title: Decision flow with if and switch statements
hook: Curly braces { } define a scope where local variables live. An if statement requires a bool condition — not a truthy number like JavaScript. A basic switch compares against constant values and never falls through without an explicit jump.

sections.heading: What are if and switch statements?

blocks.text: A **statement** is a single instruction: assign a variable, call a method, or branch with if. A **block** is a group of statements inside `{ }` that share a scope — locals declared inside are invisible outside. The **if statement** runs one branch when a bool condition is true. The **switch statement** picks a branch by comparing an expression to constant case labels. This module covers the classic switch form only; pattern matching switches come in a later module.

entries.plainDefinition: A group of statements inside curly braces { } that share a local scope.
entries.example: if (ok) { int x = 1; } — x is not visible after the closing brace.

entries.plainDefinition: A type with exactly two values: true or false. if conditions must be bool — C# will not coerce numbers or strings.
entries.example: if (count > 0) is legal; if (count) is a compile error.

entries.plainDefinition: In C, execution drops from one case into the next. C# forbids this unless you write goto case explicitly.
entries.example: case 1: DoWork(); goto case 2; — the only legal fall-through.

blocks.text: Requiring bool in if conditions eliminates a whole class of bugs that plague JavaScript developers. You cannot write if (retries) — you must write if (retries > 0). This is intentional: the compiler catches mistakes at build time instead of letting a zero slip through as false at run time. Always use braces around if/else bodies, even for a single statement — dangling else bugs are real.

blocks.title: Real-world use case
blocks.body: Use if/else chains for auth-provider branching (LTI versus local) when the discriminator is a simple string or enum constant. Use a classic switch when you have many constant cases and want a clear dispatch table.

sections.heading: How if and switch execute step by step

items.title: Evaluate the condition
items.body: The expression inside if ( ) must produce a bool. No truthy coercion.

items.title: Enter the matching block
items.body: If true, run the if block. If false, check else if chains or run else.

items.title: Exit the scope
items.body: Locals declared inside the block are destroyed when the block ends.

diagram.title: Classic switch dispatch
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Evaluate switch expression] --> B{Match case label?}
  B -->|case lti| C[Run lti branch]
  B -->|case local| D[Run local branch]
  B -->|default| E[Run default branch]
  C --> F[break / return / throw]
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F --> G[Exit switch]

sections.heading: Code walkthrough: if, else, and switch

snippet.label: if requires bool; basic switch on a token issuer
snippet.explanation: Classic switch needs break (or return/throw/goto case) to avoid falling through. goto case is the explicit fall-through. Pattern switches come in module 11.

snippet.label: Block scope and definite assignment
snippet.explanation: Blocks control variable lifetime. The compiler tracks definite assignment — every path must assign a local before you read it.

snippet.label: Stacked case labels and goto case
snippet.explanation: Stacked case labels (case 200: case 201:) are not fall-through of statements — they are multiple labels on one section. Statement fall-through still needs goto case.

blocks.title: C# vs JavaScript/TypeScript control flow
rows: Falls through by default in JS
let/const block scope; var function scope

blocks.title: Top pitfalls
blocks.body: Writing if (count) after years of JavaScript — it does not compile. Omitting break and expecting implicit fall-through like C. Using a switch expression in an interview while claiming you have not covered patterns yet. Skipping braces on single-line if bodies and creating a dangling else.

interviewTakeaways: if conditions are bool only; C# will not coerce numbers or strings.
Classic switch is equality to constants plus mandatory break (or another jump).
Blocks control definite assignment and lifetime of locals.
goto case is the only legal way to fall through between switch cases.
commonPitfalls: Writing if (count) after years of JavaScript — it does not compile.
Omitting break and expecting implicit fall-through like C.
Using a switch expression in an interview while claiming you have not covered patterns yet.
Declaring locals outside a block when they are only needed inside — pollutes scope.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript if (x) is truthy. C# if (x) needs bool. JavaScript switch falls through by default; C# requires an explicit jump like break or goto case.
